One-pager

  • MOTION IN A STRAIGHT LINE
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • DISTANCE vs DISPLACEMENT
  • Displacement joins the initial point to the final point
  • Distance is the length of the arc, r theta
  • Displacement is 2r sine theta by 2
  • 2
  • VELOCITY
  • Rate of change of displacement, rate of change in position
  • Velocity = displacement by time
  • Speed = distance by time
  • 3
  • ACCELERATION
  • The rate of change in velocity is called acceleration
  • 4
  • TYPES OF MOTION
  • Uniform motion: constant velocity
  • Uniform acceleration: velocity changes at a steady rate
  • Variable acceleration: acceleration itself changes
  • 5
  • SIGN OF ACCELERATION
  • If acceleration is positive, velocity increases
  • If acceleration is negative, velocity decreases
  • 6
  • RETARDING MOTION
  • Velocity and acceleration point in opposite directions
  • 7
  • MOTION UNDER GRAVITY
  • This is uniform acceleration
  • Acceleration due to gravity is 9.8, directed downwards
  • 8
  • AVERAGE VELOCITY
  • Average velocity is always total displacement by total time
(Memory Note) Distance follows the path, displacement joins the ends.
(Memory Note) Speed uses distance, velocity uses displacement.
(Memory Note) Acceleration measures how fast velocity itself changes.
(Memory Note) Uniform means constant, variable means changing.
(Memory Note) The sign tells you speeding up or slowing down.
(Memory Note) Opposite directions always means slowing down.
(Memory Note) Free fall is just uniform acceleration pointing down.
(Memory Note) Average velocity is never the average of two velocities.

Motion in a straight line — One-pager

Acceleration

  • ACCELERATION
  • The rate of change in velocity is called acceleration
(Memory Note) Acceleration measures how fast the velocity itself is changing.
🃏
Image coming
Motion in a straight line
Acceleration

Average Velocity

  • AVERAGE VELOCITY
  • Average velocity is always TOTAL DISPLACEMENT by TOTAL TIME
(Memory Note) Never average the two velocities — always total displacement over total time.
🃏
Image coming
Motion in a straight line
Average Velocity

Calculus Form

  • CALCULUS FORM
  • v = dx by dt
  • Velocity is the derivative of position
  • Variable acceleration means a is a function of t
(Memory Note) Differentiate position to get velocity, then velocity to get acceleration.
🃏
Image coming
Motion in a straight line
Calculus Form

DISTANCE vs DISPLACEMENT

  • DISTANCE vs DISPLACEMENT
  • DISPLACEMENT joins the initial point and the final point
  • DISTANCE is the length of the arc, r theta
  • Displacement is 2r sine theta by 2
(Memory Note) Distance follows the path; displacement only joins the two ends.
🃏
Image coming
Motion in a straight line
DISTANCE vs DISPLACEMENT

Motion Under Gravity

  • MOTION UNDER GRAVITY
  • Motion under gravity is uniform acceleration
  • Acceleration due to gravity is 9.8, directed downwards
(Memory Note) Free fall is just uniform acceleration pointing straight down.
🃏
Image coming
Motion in a straight line
Motion Under Gravity

Sign Of Acceleration

  • SIGN OF ACCELERATION
  • If acceleration is POSITIVE, velocity increases
  • If acceleration is NEGATIVE, velocity decreases
  • RETARDING MOTION: velocity and acceleration are in opposite directions
(Memory Note) Opposite directions always means slowing down.
🃏
Image coming
Motion in a straight line
Sign Of Acceleration

Uniform And Variable Motion

  • UNIFORM AND VARIABLE MOTION
  • UNIFORM MOTION: a particle moving with constant velocity
  • UNIFORM ACCELERATION: the velocity changes at a steady rate
  • VARIABLE ACCELERATION: the acceleration itself changes
(Memory Note) Uniform means constant; variable means changing.
🃏
Image coming
Motion in a straight line
Uniform And Variable Motion

Velocity And Speed

  • VELOCITY AND SPEED
  • VELOCITY is the rate of change of displacement
  • Velocity = displacement by time
  • SPEED = distance by time
(Memory Note) Speed uses distance, velocity uses displacement — that is the only difference.

  • TWO AXES, STUDIED SEPARATELY
  • x and y are always perpendicular
  • x is displacement along the x axis, y is displacement along the y axis
  • 2
  • COMPONENT VELOCITIES
  • Vx = dx by dt
  • Vy = dy by dt
  • 3
  • NET VELOCITY
  • Net velocity = root over Vx square plus Vy square
  • 4
  • DIRECTION
  • tan theta = Vy by Vx
  • 5
  • VECTOR FORM
  • Velocity vector = dr bar by dt
  • 6
  • PROJECTILE: HORIZONTAL
  • No acceleration in the horizontal direction
  • Horizontal velocity is always u cos theta
  • 7
  • PROJECTILE: VERTICAL
  • Acceleration acts downward in the vertical direction
  • Velocity decreases going up and increases coming down
  • 8
  • HORIZONTAL DISPLACEMENT
  • x = u cos theta into t

One-pager

  • MOTION IN A PLANE
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • TWO AXES, STUDIED SEPARATELY
  • x and y are always perpendicular
  • x axis and y axis should be read separately
  • 2
  • COMPONENT VELOCITIES
  • Along x axis, Vx = dx by dt
  • Along y axis, Vy = dy by dt
  • 3
  • NET VELOCITY
  • Net velocity = root over Vx square plus Vy square
  • 4
  • DIRECTION OF VELOCITY
  • tan theta = Vy by Vx
  • 5
  • VECTOR FORM
  • Position vector written with i cap and j cap
  • Velocity vector = dr bar by dt
  • 6
  • PROJECTILE, HORIZONTAL DIRECTION
  • There is no acceleration in the horizontal direction
  • The horizontal velocity is always u cos theta
  • 7
  • PROJECTILE, VERTICAL DIRECTION
  • Acceleration acts downward in the vertical direction
  • Velocity decreases on the way up, then increases on the way down
  • 8
  • HORIZONTAL DISPLACEMENT
  • When there is no acceleration, distance = speed into time
  • x = u cos theta into t
(Memory Note) Two separate one-dimensional problems, solved side by side.
(Memory Note) Differentiate each coordinate on its own.
(Memory Note) Pythagoras works because x and y are perpendicular.
(Memory Note) The ratio of the components gives the angle.
(Memory Note) Differentiating the position vector gives the velocity vector.
(Memory Note) Nothing pushes sideways, so horizontal velocity never changes.
(Memory Note) Only the vertical motion feels gravity.
(Memory Note) Horizontal distance is just constant speed times time.

Horizontal Displacement

  • HORIZONTAL DISPLACEMENT
  • When there is no acceleration, distance = speed into time
  • x = u cos theta into t

Horizontal Displacement

Net Velocity

  • NET VELOCITY
  • Net velocity = root over Vx square plus Vy square
  • This works because x and y are always perpendicular
(Memory Note) Pythagoras works only because the two axes are at right angles.

Net Velocity

Projectile — Horizontal Direction

  • PROJECTILE — HORIZONTAL DIRECTION
  • There is NO ACCELERATION in the horizontal direction
  • The horizontal velocity is always u cos theta
(Memory Note) Nothing pushes sideways, so the horizontal velocity never changes.

  • PROJECTILE — VERTICAL DIRECTION
  • Acceleration acts downward in the vertical direction
  • The velocity decreases going up and increases coming down

  • y is displacement along the y axis
  • The x axis and y axis should be read separately

Why Atoms Bond

  • WHY ATOMS BOND
  • POTENTIAL ENERGY
  • INTER NUCLEAR DISTANCE
  • Bond is formed at minimum energy
  • Bond length
  • MINIMUM ENERGY
  • Bond length is reduced
  • Bond strength increases
(Memory Note) The bond sits exactly at the lowest point of the curve.
🃏
Image coming
chemical bonding
Why Atoms Bond

The Octet Rule

  • THE OCTET RULE
  • 8 ELECTRONS
  • Every atom has a tendency to complete 8 electrons in its valency shell
  • TRANSFER
  • One atom gives, one atom takes
  • SHARE
  • Both atoms share a pair
(Memory Note) Transfer or share — the goal is always 8.
🃏
Image coming
chemical bonding
The Octet Rule

Lewis Dot Structure

  • LEWIS DOT STRUCTURE
  • STEP 1
  • Draw valence electrons as dots
  • STEP 2
  • Place the surrounding atoms
  • STEP 3
  • Count the number of bonds required
  • Shared pairs become bond lines
  • Remaining dots stay as lone pairs
(Memory Note) Number of bonds required decides the structure.
🃏

chemical bonding
Lewis Dot Structure

Formal Charge

  • FORMAL CHARGE
  • VALENCE ELECTRONS
  • LONE PAIR ELECTRONS
  • BONDING ELECTRONS
  • Three bonds means six electrons
  • Formal charge is very easy
(Memory Note) Count all three, every single time.

  • INCOMPLETE OCTET
  • BF3
  • BCl3
  • 6 ELECTRONS
  • Boron has only 6 electrons
  • ELECTRON DEFICIENT
  • Hypo means less
  • These still exist
(Memory Note) Hypovalent = fewer than 8, and still stable.

  • 12 ELECTRONS
  • These also have existence

  • But they exist
  • At least one unpaired electron

Sigma And Pi Bonds

  • SIGMA
  • Formed first, along the axis
  • PI
  • Formed above and below the axis
  • One sigma and two pi bonds
  • TRIPLE BOND

Mind map

  • LAWS OF MOTION
  • JEE Crash · GenZ 2.O
  • 1
  • FIRST LAW: INERTIA
  • An object at rest cannot move by itself
  • It cannot move unless an external force acts on it
  • 2
  • SECOND LAW
  • External force = rate of change of linear momentum
  • 3
  • LINEAR MOMENTUM
  • P = mass into velocity
  • F = dP by dt
  • 4
  • AVERAGE FORCE
  • Force calculated over a time interval is called average force
  • 5
  • F = ma
  • Acceleration a = F by m
  • 6
  • TENSION
  • Whatever force is applied through a string is the tension
  • 7
  • EQUILIBRIUM
  • The net force on the body must be zero
  • 8
  • DIRECTION
  • tan theta = y component divided by x component
(Memory Note) The second law is really F = dP by dt — F = ma is the special case.

LAWS OF MOTION
LAWS OF MOTION — Mind map

One-pager

  • LAWS OF MOTION
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • FIRST LAW, INERTIA
  • The object at rest cannot move by itself
  • This is called inertia
  • It cannot move by itself unless an external force is acting on it
  • 2
  • SECOND LAW
  • Whenever there is an external force acting on a body, that external force is equal to the rate of change in linear momentum
  • 3
  • LINEAR MOMENTUM
  • Linear momentum P = mass into velocity
  • F = dP by dt
  • 4
  • AVERAGE FORCE
  • A force calculated over a time interval is called average force
  • 5
  • F = ma
  • After knowing F = ma, acceleration a = F by m
  • 6
  • TENSION IN A STRING
  • Whatever force is applied through the string is the tension
  • The tension always tries to pull
  • 7
  • EQUILIBRIUM
  • What does equilibrium mean? The net force on it should be zero
  • 8
  • DIRECTION OF A FORCE
  • tan theta = y component divided by x component
(Memory Note) No external force means no change in motion.
(Memory Note) The real second law is about momentum, not just mass times acceleration.
(Memory Note) Momentum carries both mass and velocity.
(Memory Note) Instantaneous force uses dP by dt; average force uses delta P by delta t.
(Memory Note) Divide the net force by the total mass.
(Memory Note) Tension pulls, it never pushes.
(Memory Note) Equilibrium means the forces cancel exactly.
(Memory Note) Same rule as for any vector.

  • A force calculated over a TIME INTERVAL is called AVERAGE FORCE

First Law And Inertia

  • FIRST LAW AND INERTIA
  • The object at rest cannot move by itself
  • This is called INERTIA
  • It cannot move by itself unless an EXTERNAL FORCE is acting on it
(Memory Note) No external force means no change in motion.

LAWS OF MOTION
First Law And Inertia

Second Law And Momentum

  • SECOND LAW AND MOMENTUM
  • Whenever there is an external force acting on a body, that external force is equal to the RATE OF CHANGE IN LINEAR MOMENTUM
  • LINEAR MOMENTUM P = mass into velocity
  • F = dP by dt
(Memory Note) The real second law is about momentum, not just mass times acceleration.

Tension In A String

  • TENSION IN A STRING
  • Whatever force is applied through the string is the TENSION
  • F = ma, or T = ma for the pulled mass
  • The tension always tries to pull
(Memory Note) Tension pulls, it never pushes.

  • COORDINATION COMPOUNDS
  • JEE Crash · GenZ 2.O

  • COORDINATION SPHERE
  • The part inside the square bracket
  • 2
  • COUNTER ION
  • The part written outside the square bracket
  • 3
  • THE AgNO3 TEST
  • Only the counter ions precipitate
  • If 1 mole of AgCl forms, only 1 chlorine is outside the bracket
  • 4
  • CHARGE BALANCE
  • The charge must be balanced in a coordination compound
  • This holds whether it is a cation or an anion
(Memory Note) Only what is OUTSIDE the square bracket can be precipitated.

One-pager

  • COORDINATION COMPOUNDS
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • COORDINATION SPHERE
  • The name in the square bracket is called the coordination sphere
  • 2
  • COUNTER ION
  • The chlorine outside the bracket is called the counter ion
  • 3
  • THE SILVER NITRATE TEST
  • If cobalt chloride reacts with AgNO3 and produces only 1 mole of AgCl
  • then only 1 chlorine is actually outside the coordination sphere
  • Even though 3 chlorines appear in the compound
  • 4
  • CHARGE BALANCE
  • The charge should be balanced in a coordination compound
  • Whether it is a cation or an anion, the charge balance should be there
(Memory Note) Everything inside the bracket is bonded to the metal.
(Memory Note) Outside the bracket means free in solution.
(Memory Note) The test counts only the ionisable chlorines.
(Memory Note) Total charge inside plus outside must come to the overall charge.

Charge Balance

  • CHARGE BALANCE
  • The charge should be BALANCED in a coordination compound
  • Whether it is a cation or an anion, the charge balance should be there
(Memory Note) Total charge inside plus outside must give the overall charge.

Charge Balance

Coordination Sphere And Counter Ion

  • COORDINATION SPHERE AND COUNTER ION
  • The name in the SQUARE BRACKET is called the COORDINATION SPHERE
  • The chlorine written OUTSIDE is called the COUNTER ION
(Memory Note) Inside the bracket is bonded to the metal; outside is free in solution.
🃏
Image coming
coordination compounds
Coordination Sphere And Counter Ion

The Silver Nitrate Test

  • THE SILVER NITRATE TEST
  • If cobalt chloride reacts with AgNO3, it produces only 1 MOLE of AgCl
  • There are 3 chlorines in the compound, but only 1 mole precipitates
  • That tells you only 1 chlorine is outside the coordination sphere
(Memory Note) The test counts only the ionisable chlorines, not all of them.

  • Work is the scalar product of force and displacement
  • Work done = F s cos theta
  • 2

  • theta = 90 degrees: work done = 0
  • theta = 180 degrees: work done is negative

WORK, ENERGY & POWER
WORK, ENERGY & POWER — Mind map

One-pager

  • WORK, ENERGY & POWER
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • WORK DONE
  • Work is the scalar product of force and displacement
  • The basic formula is work done = force into displacement
  • Work done = F s cos theta
  • 2
  • ANGLE = 0 DEGREES
  • Force and displacement in the same direction
  • Work done = Fs
  • 3
  • ANGLE = 90 DEGREES
  • Force perpendicular to displacement
  • Work done = Fs cos 90 = 0
  • 4
  • ANGLE = 180 DEGREES
  • Force opposite to displacement
  • Work done = Fs cos 180 degrees
  • cos 180 is minus 1, so the work done is negative
  • 5
  • UNITS OF WORK
  • 1 Joule = 10 to the power 7 erg
  • 6
  • WORK-ENERGY THEOREM
  • Work done by all the forces is equal to the change in kinetic energy
  • 7
  • TENSION DOES NO WORK
  • Tension force and displacement are at 90 degrees
  • cos 90 is 0, so work done by tension is 0
  • 8
  • WORK DONE BY GRAVITY
  • mgh into cos 180 degrees
  • cos 180 is minus 1
(Memory Note) Always check the angle before using Fs.
(Memory Note) Maximum positive work.
(Memory Note) A perpendicular force does no work at all.
(Memory Note) Opposing force means negative work.
(Memory Note) Joule is SI, erg is the CGS unit.
(Memory Note) Add up every force first, then equate to the change in KE.
(Memory Note) In a pendulum the string never does any work.
(Memory Note) Lifting against gravity gives negative work by gravity.

WORK, ENERGY & POWER
WORK, ENERGY & POWER — One-pager

Tension Does No Work

  • TENSION DOES NO WORK
  • Tension force and displacement are at 90 DEGREES
  • cos 90 is 0, so the work done by tension is 0
(Memory Note) In a pendulum, the string never does any work.
🃏
Image coming
WORK, ENERGY & POWER
Tension Does No Work

The Three Angles

  • THE THREE ANGLES
  • theta = 0 DEGREES: force and displacement same direction, work done = Fs
  • theta = 90 DEGREES: work done = Fs cos 90, which is 0
  • theta = 180 DEGREES: work done = Fs cos 180 degrees, which is negative
(Memory Note) Same direction positive, perpendicular zero, opposite negative.
🃏
Image coming
WORK, ENERGY & POWER
The Three Angles

Units Of Work

  • UNITS OF WORK
  • 1 JOULE = 10 TO THE POWER 7 ERG
(Memory Note) Joule is the SI unit, erg is the CGS unit.
🃏
Image coming
WORK, ENERGY & POWER
Units Of Work

Work Done By Gravity

  • WORK DONE BY GRAVITY
  • Work done by gravity = mgh into cos 180 degrees
  • cos 180 is minus 1
(Memory Note) Lifting a body gives negative work done by gravity.
🃏
Image coming
WORK, ENERGY & POWER
Work Done By Gravity

Work Done — The Formula

  • WORK DONE — THE FORMULA
  • Work is the SCALAR PRODUCT of force and displacement
  • Work done = force into displacement
  • Work done = F s cos theta
(Memory Note) Work needs force, displacement, and the angle between them.
🃏
Image coming
WORK, ENERGY & POWER
Work Done — The Formula

Work-Energy Theorem

  • WORK-ENERGY THEOREM
  • Work done by ALL THE FORCES is equal to the CHANGE IN KINETIC ENERGY
(Memory Note) Every force counts — add them all up before equating.

Mind map

  • ROTATIONAL MOTION
  • JEE Crash · GenZ 2.O
  • 1
  • MASS DENSITIES
  • Linear mass density lambda = M by L, mass per unit length
  • Surface density = m by A
  • Volume density = m by V
  • 2
  • CENTRE OF MASS, TWO BODIES
  • M2 R2 = M1 R1 when the reference point is taken at the centre
  • 3
  • VELOCITY OF CENTRE OF MASS
  • m1v1 plus m2v2 and so on, divided by total mass
  • 4
  • ZERO NET FORCE
  • If F net on the body is zero, acceleration of the centre of mass is zero
  • For two masses, m1 a1 = minus m2 a2
  • 5
  • TORQUE
  • Torque is r cross F, a cross product
  • 6
  • THE LINEAR-ANGULAR ANALOGY
  • L = I omega, the twin of P = mv
  • Tau = I alpha, the twin of F = ma
  • 7

  • Tau = dL by dt

  • For discs of the same material and thickness, mass is proportional to R squared, so I is proportional to R to the power 4

ROTATIONAL MOTION
ROTATIONAL MOTION — One-pager

Angular Momentum

  • ANGULAR MOMENTUM
  • L = I omega
  • This is the rotational analog of linear momentum, P = mv
  • Torque, tau = I alpha
  • This is the rotational analog of F = ma
  • Kinetic energy = half I omega square
  • This is the rotational analog of half mv square
(Memory Note) Swap m for I and v for omega — every linear formula has a rotational twin.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Angular Momentum

Centre Of Mass Of Two Bodies

  • CENTRE OF MASS OF TWO BODIES
  • M2 R2 = M1 R1
  • This holds when the reference point of the system is taken at the centre
(Memory Note) The heavier mass always sits closer to the centre of mass.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Centre Of Mass Of Two Bodies

Conservation Of Angular Momentum

  • CONSERVATION OF ANGULAR MOMENTUM
  • F = dP by dt for linear motion
  • Torque = dL by dt for rotational motion
  • This is used for conservation of angular momentum
  • When we find the net torque, we use this concept
(Memory Note) Zero net torque means L stays constant — the rotational twin of zero net force keeping P constant.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Conservation Of Angular Momentum

Mass Densities

  • MASS DENSITIES
  • LINEAR mass density lambda = M by L, mass per unit length
  • SURFACE density = m by A, mass per unit area
  • VOLUME density = m by V
(Memory Note) Pick the density that matches the shape — line, sheet or solid.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Mass Densities

Moment Of Inertia — The Disc Trap

  • MOMENT OF INERTIA — THE DISC TRAP
  • For two discs of the SAME MATERIAL AND THICKNESS
  • Mass is directly proportional to r square
  • So moment of inertia is directly proportional to R TO THE POWER 4
  • I1 by I2 = R1 by R2 whole to the power 4
  • Writing I1 by I2 = R1 by R2 whole square here is completely wrong
(Memory Note) Same material and thickness is the condition — without it, R to the power 4 does not hold.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Moment Of Inertia — The Disc Trap

Moment Of Inertia — The Sphere

  • MOMENT OF INERTIA — THE SPHERE
  • Mass is directly proportional to volume
  • Volume of a sphere is 4 by 3 pi r cube, so mass is proportional to r cube
  • I1 by I2 = R1 by R2 whole to the power 5
(Memory Note) Mass itself grows with radius, so the power climbs to five.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Moment Of Inertia — The Sphere

Parallel Axis Theorem

  • PARALLEL AXIS THEOREM
  • For a disc about its centre of mass, I = m r square by 2
  • About an axis TANGENT TO THE DISC and PERPENDICULAR TO ITS PLANE
  • add m r square for the distance moved
  • I (tangential) = m r square by 2 plus m r square
  • Which equals 3 by 2, m r square
(Memory Note) Parallel axis: take I about the centre of mass, then add m times the distance-squared to the new axis.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Parallel Axis Theorem

Torque As A Cross Product

  • TORQUE AS A CROSS PRODUCT
  • Torque is r cross F
  • This is a cross product, not a dot product
(Memory Note) Cross product means the direction matters, not just the size.
🃏
Image coming
ROTATIONAL MOTION
Torque As A Cross Product

Velocity Of The Centre Of Mass

  • VELOCITY OF THE CENTRE OF MASS
  • m1v1 plus m2v2 plus m3v3 and so on up to mn vn
  • divided by m1 plus m2 and so on, the total mass
(Memory Note) It is a mass-weighted average of all the velocities.
🃏

Velocity Of The Centre Of Mass

When Net Force Is Zero

  • WHEN NET FORCE IS ZERO
  • If F net acting on the body is zero, the acceleration of the centre of mass is zero
  • For a system of two masses, m1 a1 = minus m2 a2
(Memory Note) No external force means the centre of mass cannot accelerate.

Atomic Number

  • ATOMIC NUMBER
  • Atomic number is the number of PROTONS in the nucleus of an atom
  • For a NEUTRAL ATOM, it is the number of protons present in the nucleus
(Memory Note) Atomic number counts protons only.

Atomic Number

Bohrs Second Postulate

  • BOHRS SECOND POSTULATE
  • Angular momentum = nh BY 2 PI
  • Angular momentum is an INTEGRAL MULTIPLE of h by 2 pi
(Memory Note) Only whole-number multiples are allowed — that is what quantised means.

Energy In A Bohr Orbit

  • ENERGY IN A BOHR ORBIT
  • Generally, energy should be lost
  • But in a BOHR ORBIT, energy is NOT lost
(Memory Note) A stationary orbit does not radiate energy away.

One-pager

  • GRAVITATION
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • NEWTONS LAW OF GRAVITATION
  • The force between two masses is directly proportional to the product of the masses
  • Inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
  • And acts along the line joining them
  • 2
  • THE FORMULA
  • F = G m1 m2 by R square
  • 3
  • THE GRAVITATIONAL CONSTANT
  • G = 6.67 into 10 to the power minus 11 newton metre square per kg square
  • 4
  • MUTUAL FORCE
  • The force between two masses is called a mutual force
  • 5
  • PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION
  • Force is a vector quantity, so forces cannot be added directly
  • They must be added using vector laws
  • 6
  • KEPLER, LAW OF ORBITS
  • All the planets revolve around the sun in elliptical orbits
  • 7
  • KEPLER, LAW OF AREAS
  • The areal velocity is constant
  • The rate of change of area is L by 2m
  • a1 by t1 = a2 by t2
  • 8
  • CONSERVED QUANTITIES
  • The total energy of the planet always remains constant
  • Angular momentum is conserved when there is no external force
(Memory Note) Three parts: product of masses, inverse square, along the joining line.
(Memory Note) R is the distance between the two masses.
(Memory Note) G is tiny, which is why gravity is weak between everyday objects.
(Memory Note) Each mass pulls the other equally.
(Memory Note) Add gravitational forces as vectors, never as plain numbers.
(Memory Note) Orbits are ellipses, not circles.
(Memory Note) Equal areas are swept in equal times.
(Memory Note) Both energy and angular momentum stay constant in orbit.

Conserved Quantities In Orbit

  • CONSERVED QUANTITIES IN ORBIT
  • The TOTAL ENERGY of the planet always remains constant
  • Angular momentum is conserved when there is no external force
  • This is called conservation of angular momentum
(Memory Note) Both energy and angular momentum stay constant all the way round the orbit.

  • KEPLER — LAW OF AREAS
  • The AREAL VELOCITY is constant
  • Areal velocity is area by time
  • The rate of change of area is L by 2m
  • a1 by t1 = a2 by t2
(Memory Note) Equal areas are swept out in equal times.

Newton'S Law Of Gravitation

  • NEWTON'S LAW OF GRAVITATION
  • The force between two masses is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to the product of the masses
  • INVERSELY PROPORTIONAL to the square of the distance between them
  • And acts ALONG THE LINE joining them
  • This is called a mutual force
(Memory Note) Three parts: product of masses, inverse square, along the joining line.

  • PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION
  • Force is a VECTOR quantity
  • So we cannot add the forces directly
  • We have to use vector laws
(Memory Note) Add gravitational forces as vectors, never as plain numbers.

  • F = G m1 m2 by R square
  • G = 6.67 INTO 10 TO THE POWER MINUS 11
  • Units: newton metre square per kg square
(Memory Note) G is tiny, which is why gravity is weak between everyday objects.

Mind map

  • SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION
  • JEE Crash · GenZ 2.O
  • 1
  • FREQUENCY
  • The reciprocal of time period is called frequency
  • Frequency is the number of cycles per second
  • 2
  • RESTORING FORCE
  • F = minus K into X to the power N
  • This is called the restoring force
  • 3
  • THE CONDITION FOR SHM
  • The power of x must be an ODD number
  • Then F = minus kx is the restoring force acting on the body
  • 4
  • EXTREME POSITIONS
  • x = 0 at the mean position
  • x = plus a and x = minus a at the extremes
  • 5
  • THE EQUATION
  • x = a sine omega t when the particle starts from the mean position
  • 6
  • ANGULAR SHM
  • Theta naught stands for angular amplitude
  • 7
  • LINEAR AND ANGULAR LINK
  • v = L into omega, where omega is the angular velocity
(Memory Note) The minus sign in F = minus kx is what makes the motion oscillate.

One-pager

  • SIMPLE HARMONIC MOTION
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • TIME PERIOD AND FREQUENCY
  • The reciprocal of time period is called frequency of oscillation
  • Frequency is the number of cycles per second
  • 2
  • RESTORING FORCE
  • The nature of force for oscillatory motion is F = minus K into X to the power N
  • This is called the restoring force
  • 3
  • THE CONDITION FOR SHM
  • The power of x must be an odd number
  • Then F = minus kx is the restoring force acting on the body
  • 4
  • POSITIONS IN LINEAR SHM
  • x = 0 is the mean position
  • x = plus a and x = minus a are the two extreme positions
  • 5
  • THE DISPLACEMENT EQUATION
  • If the particle starts from the mean position, x = a sine omega t
  • 6
  • ANGULAR SHM
  • Theta naught stands for angular amplitude
  • The equation is almost the same as linear SHM
  • 7
  • LINEAR AND ANGULAR LINK
  • v = L into omega
  • Omega stands for angular velocity
(Memory Note) Frequency and time period are reciprocals of each other.
(Memory Note) The minus sign is what pulls the body back towards the centre.
(Memory Note) Odd power only — this is the condition the teacher stresses.
(Memory Note) The particle travels from one extreme to the other through the centre.
(Memory Note) Starting point decides whether you use sine or cosine.
(Memory Note) Swap displacement for angle and the form stays identical.
(Memory Note) Multiply angular velocity by the radius to get linear speed.

Angular Shm

  • ANGULAR SHM
  • Theta naught stands for ANGULAR AMPLITUDE
  • The equation is almost the same as linear SHM
(Memory Note) Swap displacement for angle and the form stays identical.

Simple Harmonic Motion
Angular Shm

Linear And Angular Link

  • LINEAR AND ANGULAR LINK
  • v = L into omega
  • Omega stands for ANGULAR VELOCITY
(Memory Note) Multiply angular velocity by the radius to get the linear speed.
🃏
Image coming
Simple Harmonic Motion
Linear And Angular Link

Positions In Linear Shm

  • POSITIONS IN LINEAR SHM
  • x = 0 is the MEAN POSITION
  • x = plus a and x = minus a are the two EXTREME POSITIONS
  • The particle travels from one extreme position to the other
(Memory Note) The centre is where speed is highest and force is zero.
🃏
Image coming
Simple Harmonic Motion
Positions In Linear Shm

Restoring Force

  • RESTORING FORCE
  • The nature of force for oscillatory motion is F = minus K into X to the power N
  • This is called the RESTORING FORCE
(Memory Note) The minus sign is what pulls the body back towards the centre.
🃏
Image coming
Simple Harmonic Motion
Restoring Force

The Condition For Shm

  • THE CONDITION FOR SHM
  • The power of x must be an ODD NUMBER
  • Then F = minus kx is the restoring force acting on the body
(Memory Note) Odd power only — that is the condition for simple harmonic motion.
🃏
Image coming
Simple Harmonic Motion
The Condition For Shm

The Displacement Equation

  • THE DISPLACEMENT EQUATION
  • If the particle starts from the mean position, x = a sine omega t
(Memory Note) Where the particle starts decides whether you use sine or cosine.
🃏
Image coming
Simple Harmonic Motion
The Displacement Equation

Time Period And Frequency

  • TIME PERIOD AND FREQUENCY
  • The RECIPROCAL of time period is called FREQUENCY of oscillation
  • Frequency is the number of cycles per second
  • The number of times it repeats in 1 second is called frequency
(Memory Note) Frequency and time period are reciprocals of each other.

  • DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM
  • Rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction
  • Relative movement is zero, but the reaction has not stopped
  • 2
  • LAW OF MASS ACTION
  • Kc = products concentration to the power of their coefficients, divided by reactants concentration to the power of their coefficients
  • 3
  • Kp AND Kc
  • Kp = Kc(RT) to the power delta n
  • Units of Kc are mol/L to the power delta n, units of Kp are atm to the power delta n
  • 4
  • GIBBS FREE ENERGY
  • Delta G = 0 at equilibrium
  • Delta G less than 0 is spontaneous, greater than 0 is non-spontaneous
  • 5
  • CATALYST
  • Speeds up the approach to equilibrium, but does not shift it
  • 6
  • REACTION QUOTIENT
  • Qc less than Kc: forward
  • Qc greater than Kc: backward
  • Qc equal to Kc: at equilibrium
  • 7
  • HOMOGENEOUS vs HETEROGENEOUS
  • Same phase throughout = homogeneous, different phases = heterogeneous
  • 8
  • LE CHATELIER
  • Increase reactant concentration: forward
  • Increase product concentration: backward
  • High temperature favours endothermic
  • High pressure favours fewer gas moles
(Memory Note) Whatever change you make, equilibrium shifts to oppose it.

One-pager

  • CHEMICAL EQUILIBRIUM
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM
  • Two opposite processes occur at the same rate
  • Rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction
  • 2
  • LAW OF MASS ACTION — Kc
  • Kc = products concentration to the power of coefficients, over reactants concentration to the power of coefficients
  • 3
  • Kp AND THE Kp-Kc RELATION
  • Kp = Kc(RT) to the power delta n
  • Delta n is product gas moles minus reactant gas moles
  • Units of Kc are mol/L to the power delta n
  • Units of Kp are atm to the power delta n
  • 4
  • GIBBS FREE ENERGY
  • Delta G less than 0: spontaneous
  • Delta G greater than 0: non-spontaneous
  • Delta G equal to 0: equilibrium
  • 5
  • CATALYST
  • Changes the rate of reaction and the rate of approach to equilibrium
  • Does not change the state of equilibrium
  • 6
  • REACTION QUOTIENT, Q
  • Qc less than Kc: reaction goes forward
  • Qc greater than Kc: reaction goes backward
  • Qc equal to Kc: already at equilibrium
  • 7
  • HOMOGENEOUS vs HETEROGENEOUS
  • Homogeneous: all reactants and products in the same phase
  • Heterogeneous: reactants and products in different phases
  • 8
  • LE CHATELIER PRINCIPLE
  • Increase reactant concentration: shifts forward
  • Increase product concentration: shifts backward
  • High temperature favours the endothermic direction, delta H greater than 0
  • Low or moderate temperature favours the exothermic direction, delta H less than 0
  • High pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles
  • Low pressure favours the side with more gas moles
  • For ammonia, N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3, delta H is minus 92 kilojoule per mole
(Memory Note) Movement never stops — it is just equal in both directions.
(Memory Note) Products on top, reactants on the bottom.
(Memory Note) A pure solid or liquid has no concentration term — it counts as 1.
(Memory Note) At equilibrium, delta G is exactly zero.
(Memory Note) A catalyst speeds up the trip, not the destination.
(Memory Note) Q is K calculated before equilibrium is reached.
(Memory Note) Same phase throughout = homogeneous.
(Memory Note) The system always opposes whatever change you make.

Ammonia Production

  • AMMONIA PRODUCTION
  • N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3
  • Delta H is minus 92 kilojoule per mole
  • This is an exothermic reaction
(Memory Note) Negative delta H always means exothermic — heat is released.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
Ammonia Production

Catalyst And Equilibrium

  • CATALYST AND EQUILIBRIUM
  • A catalyst can alter the rate of reaction and the rate of approach to equilibrium
  • A catalyst does not change the state of equilibrium
  • 0.5 moles at equilibrium stays 0.5 moles at equilibrium, even with a catalyst
(Memory Note) A catalyst gets you there faster — it does not move the finish line.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
Catalyst And Equilibrium

Dynamic Equilibrium

  • DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM
  • Chemical equilibrium is a unique state where two opposite processes occur at the same rate
  • Rate of forward reaction equals rate of backward reaction
  • Relative movement is zero, but the reaction has not stopped
(Memory Note) Not static — forward and backward are both happening, equally.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
Dynamic Equilibrium

Gibbs Free Energy At Equilibrium

  • GIBBS FREE ENERGY AT EQUILIBRIUM
  • Delta G measures spontaneity
  • A spontaneous reaction has delta G less than 0
  • A non-spontaneous reaction has delta G greater than 0
  • At equilibrium, delta G equals 0
(Memory Note) Delta G = 0 at equilibrium — forward and backward are perfectly balanced.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
Gibbs Free Energy At Equilibrium

HOMOGENEOUS vs HETEROGENEOUS EQUILIBRIUM

  • HOMOGENEOUS vs HETEROGENEOUS EQUILIBRIUM
  • Homogeneous equilibrium: all reactants and products are in the same phase
  • Heterogeneous equilibrium: reactants and products are in different phases
(Memory Note) Same phase throughout = homogeneous.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
HOMOGENEOUS vs HETEROGENEOUS EQUILIBRIUM

Kp AND THE Kp-Kc RELATION

  • Kp AND THE Kp-Kc RELATION
  • Kp is the equilibrium constant in terms of partial pressure
  • Kp is defined only when at least one gas is in the reaction
  • Kp = Kc(RT) to the power delta n
  • Delta n is product moles minus reactant moles
  • Units of Kc are moles per litre to the power delta n
  • Units of Kp are atmosphere to the power delta n
  • A pure solid has concentration equal to 1, so it carries no units
(Memory Note) Delta n counts gaseous moles only — solids and liquids never count.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
Kp AND THE Kp-Kc RELATION

LAW OF MASS ACTION — Kc

  • LAW OF MASS ACTION — Kc
  • Kc is also called the concentration equilibrium constant
  • Kc equals products concentration to the power of their stoichiometric coefficients, divided by reactants concentration to the power of their stoichiometric coefficients
  • This ratio comes from the law of mass action
(Memory Note) Products on top, reactants on the bottom, each raised to its own coefficient.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
LAW OF MASS ACTION — Kc

Le Chatelier — Concentration And Temperature

  • LE CHATELIER — CONCENTRATION AND TEMPERATURE
  • Increasing reactant concentration pushes the reaction forward
  • Increasing product concentration pushes the reaction backward
  • High temperature favours an endothermic reaction, delta H greater than 0
  • Low or moderate temperature favours an exothermic reaction, delta H less than 0
(Memory Note) The system always opposes the change you make.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
Le Chatelier — Concentration And Temperature

Le Chatelier — Pressure

  • LE CHATELIER — PRESSURE
  • For N2 + 3H2 giving 2NH3, the reactant side has more gas moles than the product side
  • High pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles
  • Low pressure favours the side with more gas moles
(Memory Note) High pressure squeezes the system toward fewer gas molecules.
🃏
Image coming
chemical equilibrium
Le Chatelier — Pressure

REACTION QUOTIENT — Q vs Kc

  • REACTION QUOTIENT — Q vs Kc
  • Reaction quotient equals products concentration divided by reactants concentration, at any point in time, not necessarily at equilibrium
  • If Qc is less than Kc, the reaction moves forward
  • If Qc is greater than Kc, the reaction moves backward
  • If Qc equals Kc, the reaction is at equilibrium
(Memory Note) Q is just K calculated before equilibrium is reached.
🃏

One-pager

  • FLUID MECHANICS
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • FLUID STATICS
  • Liquid always in rest is called fluid statics
  • 2
  • PRESSURE
  • Pressure is nothing but force upon area
  • This force is always perpendicular to the object surface
  • 3
  • DENSITY OF MERCURY
  • 13.6 into 10 to the power 3 kg per m cube
  • 4
  • DENSITY OF WATER
  • 10 to the power 3 kg per m cube
  • Measured at 4 degree centigrade, where water has its maximum density
  • 5
  • RELATIVE DENSITY
  • Density of the given substance upon density of water
  • 6
  • FLUID DYNAMICS
  • Fluid dynamics is fluid in motion
  • Two types of flow: streamlined flow and turbulent flow
  • 7
  • STREAMLINED FLOW
  • At one point, every passing fluid particle has the same velocity
  • Also called laminar flow or steady flow
  • 8
  • CRITICAL VELOCITY
  • Streamlined flow is possible only if the liquid velocity does not exceed a limiting value
  • That limiting value is called the critical velocity
(Memory Note) Statics means the fluid is not moving.
(Memory Note) Only the perpendicular force counts towards pressure.
(Memory Note) Mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water.
(Memory Note) Water is densest at 4 degrees, not at 0.
(Memory Note) Relative density has no units — it is a ratio.
(Memory Note) Dynamics means the fluid is moving.
(Memory Note) Same point, same velocity, every time.
(Memory Note) Go faster than critical velocity and the flow turns turbulent.

Critical Velocity

  • CRITICAL VELOCITY
  • Streamlined flow is possible ONLY IF the liquid velocity does not exceed a limiting value
  • That limiting value is called the CRITICAL VELOCITY
(Memory Note) Go faster than critical velocity and the flow turns turbulent.

Critical Velocity

Density Of Mercury And Water

  • DENSITY OF MERCURY AND WATER
  • MERCURY: 13.6 into 10 to the power 3 kg per m cube
  • WATER: 10 to the power 3 kg per m cube
  • Water is measured at 4 DEGREE CENTIGRADE, where its density is maximum
(Memory Note) Water is densest at 4 degrees, not at 0.

Pressure In A Fluid

  • PRESSURE IN A FLUID
  • Pressure is nothing but FORCE UPON AREA
  • This force is ALWAYS PERPENDICULAR to the object surface
(Memory Note) Only the perpendicular force counts towards pressure.

Relative Density

  • RELATIVE DENSITY
  • Relative density is the density of the given substance upon the density of water

Statics And Dynamics

  • STATICS AND DYNAMICS
  • FLUID STATICS: liquid always in rest
  • FLUID DYNAMICS: fluid in motion
(Memory Note) Statics is still fluid, dynamics is moving fluid.
🃏

Statics And Dynamics

STREAMLINED vs TURBULENT FLOW

  • STREAMLINED vs TURBULENT FLOW
  • There are TWO TYPES of flow in fluid motion
  • STREAMLINED FLOW: at one point, every passing fluid particle has the same velocity
  • Also called laminar flow or steady flow
  • TURBULENT FLOW is the other type
(Memory Note) Same point, same velocity, every time — that is streamlined flow.

Mind map

  • HEAT, TEMPERATURE AND CALORIMETRY
  • JEE Crash · GenZ 2.O
  • 1
  • FIXED POINTS
  • Freezing point and boiling point define any temperature scale
  • 2
  • CELSIUS AND KELVIN
  • In Celsius there are 100 divisions
  • In Kelvin also there are 100 divisions
  • The size of one degree of change is the same in both
  • 3
  • THE GENERAL CONVERSION
  • Reading minus ice point, divided by boiling point minus freezing point, is the same for every scale
  • 4
  • CELSIUS TO FAHRENHEIT
  • K minus 273 by 100 = F minus 32 by 180
  • 5
  • THE 212 AND 32 POINTS
  • On the Fahrenheit scale, 212 minus 32 is the span
(Memory Note) Every scale conversion is the same ratio, just with different fixed points.

One-pager

  • HEAT, TEMPERATURE AND CALORIMETRY
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • FIXED POINTS OF A SCALE
  • Every temperature scale is built from a freezing point and a boiling point
  • 2
  • CELSIUS AND KELVIN
  • In the Celsius scale there are 100 divisions
  • In the Kelvin scale there are also 100 divisions
  • The degree of change is equal in both scales
  • 3
  • THE GENERAL CONVERSION RULE
  • Reading minus ice point, divided by boiling point minus freezing point
  • This ratio is the same on every scale
  • 4
  • KELVIN TO FAHRENHEIT
  • K minus 273 by 100 = F minus 32 by 180
  • 5
  • THE FAHRENHEIT SPAN
  • On the Fahrenheit scale the span is 212 minus 32
(Memory Note) Two fixed points define the whole scale.
(Memory Note) A change of 1 degree Celsius equals a change of 1 Kelvin.
(Memory Note) Set the two ratios equal and solve.
(Memory Note) 273 and 32 are the two ice points; 100 and 180 are the two spans.
(Memory Note) 212 is boiling, 32 is freezing, so the span is 180.
📄

A Custom Scale

  • A CUSTOM SCALE
  • A scale can have any fixed points
  • For example, freezing point 20 and boiling point 150 degrees
(Memory Note) The method never changes, only the two fixed numbers do.
🃏

A Custom Scale

Celsius And Kelvin Divisions

  • CELSIUS AND KELVIN DIVISIONS
  • In the CELSIUS scale there are 100 divisions
  • In the KELVIN scale there are also 100 divisions
  • The degree of change is equal to the degree of change in the other scale
(Memory Note) A change of 1 degree Celsius is exactly a change of 1 Kelvin.
🃏
Image coming
Heat temperature and calorimetry
Celsius And Kelvin Divisions

Kelvin To Fahrenheit

  • KELVIN TO FAHRENHEIT
  • K minus 273 by 100 = F minus 32 by 180
  • On the Fahrenheit scale the span is 212 minus 32
(Memory Note) 273 and 32 are the two ice points; 100 and 180 are the two spans.
🃏
Image coming
Heat temperature and calorimetry
Kelvin To Fahrenheit

The General Conversion Rule

  • THE GENERAL CONVERSION RULE
  • Reading minus the ICE POINT
  • divided by BOILING POINT minus FREEZING POINT
  • This same ratio holds on every temperature scale
(Memory Note) Set the ratio on one scale equal to the ratio on the other, then solve.

One-pager

  • THERMODYNAMICS AND THERMOCHEMISTRY
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • STATE FUNCTIONS
  • State functions are those which depend only upon the state of the system
  • Temperature, volume, pressure and number of moles are examples
  • 2
  • EXTENSIVE PROPERTIES
  • Extensive properties depend on the amount of substance
  • Volume, mass, total energy, Gibbs free energy, entropy and internal energy
  • 3
  • INTENSIVE PROPERTIES
  • Intensive properties are independent of the amount of substance
  • Temperature, pressure, density, concentration, boiling point, freezing point, viscosity
  • 4
  • INTERNAL ENERGY
  • Internal energy is the energy contained within any set of molecules
  • It can be bond energy, rotational energy, and more
  • 5
  • FIRST LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS
  • Delta U = Q + W
  • Delta U is internal energy, Q is heat, W is work done
  • 6
  • WALLS SEPARATE SYSTEM FROM SURROUNDINGS
  • A wall separates the system from the surroundings
  • There are adiabatic walls and diathermic walls
  • 7
  • FOUR TYPES OF PROCESS
  • Isothermal: temperature constant
  • Adiabatic: no heat exchange
  • Isobaric and isochoric are the other two
  • 8
  • ENTHALPY
  • Enthalpy is denoted delta H
  • It is defined only in chemical reactions at constant pressure
  • Q is defined in any type of process
  • 9
  • ENTHALPY AND REACTION TYPE
  • Delta H less than 0 means exothermic
  • Delta H greater than 0 means endothermic, energy is absorbed
(Memory Note) The path taken does not matter for a state function.
(Memory Note) More substance means a bigger value.
(Memory Note) Water always boils at 100 degrees, whether it is 2 litres or 10.
(Memory Note) Internal energy is the total energy already stored inside the molecules.
(Memory Note) Change in internal energy equals heat added plus work done on the system.
(Memory Note) The wall decides whether heat can cross it.
(Memory Note) Isothermal keeps T fixed; adiabatic keeps heat fixed at zero exchange.
(Memory Note) Delta H is heat change specifically at constant pressure.
(Memory Note) Negative enthalpy releases heat; positive enthalpy absorbs it.

Degrees Of Freedom — The Numbers

  • DEGREES OF FREEDOM — THE NUMBERS
  • MONOATOMIC = 3
  • 3 translational, no rotation, no vibration
  • DIATOMIC RIGID = 5
  • 3 translational plus 2 rotational
  • DIATOMIC NON-RIGID = 7
  • 5 plus 2 vibrational
  • TRIATOMIC RIGID = 6
  • 3 translational plus 3 rotational
  • TRIATOMIC NON-RIGID = 8
  • 6 plus 2 vibrational
(Memory Note) Remember this: 3, 5, 6 — then add 2 more for every non-rigid vibration.

Monoatomic, Diatomic, Triatomic

  • MONOATOMIC, DIATOMIC, TRIATOMIC
  • MONOATOMIC means a single atom
  • DIATOMIC has two atoms joined by a bond
  • TRIATOMIC can be linear or non-linear
  • Diatomic and triatomic molecules can be rigid or non-rigid
(Memory Note) Only non-rigid diatomic and triatomic molecules vibrate.

Monoatomic, Diatomic, Triatomic

Postulates Of Kinetic Theory

  • POSTULATES OF KINETIC THEORY
  • Gas molecules are spherical in shape
  • All gas molecules are of the same size and shape
  • Collisions between gas molecules are perfectly elastic
(Memory Note) Elastic collision means no kinetic energy is lost in a collision.

Postulates Of Kinetic Theory

The Four Gas Parameters

  • THE FOUR GAS PARAMETERS
  • PRESSURE
  • VOLUME
  • TEMPERATURE
  • NUMBER OF MOLES, n
  • The parameters used to study a gas are pressure, volume, temperature and amount of substance
(Memory Note) Any gas is described by just these four.

The Four Gas Parameters

The Ideal Gas Equation

  • THE IDEAL GAS EQUATION
  • PV = nRT
  • R IS THE UNIVERSAL GAS CONSTANT
  • R = 8.314 JOULE PER MOLE KELVIN
  • Temperature must be taken only in the Kelvin scale, never in Celsius
  • We cannot do KTG or thermodynamics without PV = nRT
(Memory Note) For quick calculation, Sameer sir uses R as 25 by 3.

The Three Speeds Of Gas Molecules

  • THE THREE SPEEDS OF GAS MOLECULES
  • VRMS, ROOT MEAN SQUARE
  • Vrms = root of 3RT by M
  • V-AVERAGE
  • V-MOST-PROBABLE
  • Vmp = root of 2RT by M
  • Vrms is greater than V-average, which is greater than V-most-probable
(Memory Note) Vrms is always the biggest of the three — it is squared before it is averaged.

  • HALOALKANES AND HALOARENES
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • NUCLEOPHILE
  • If it is donated for any reason, it is called a nucleophile
  • 2
  • SOLVOLYSIS
  • When water acts as the nucleophile, it is called solvolysis
  • 3
  • SN1 CONDITIONS
  • SN1 is favourable for a tertiary alkyl halide
  • 4
  • CARBOCATION REARRANGEMENT
  • When writing the SN1 product, rearrange the carbocation
  • Which carbocation is more stable is very important
  • 5
  • INVERSION
  • The inversion product will increase
  • 6
  • BROMINATION SELECTIVITY
  • Bromination always gives the tertiary product
(Memory Note) A nucleophile donates its electron pair.
(Memory Note) Solvent acting as the nucleophile gives solvolysis.
(Memory Note) Tertiary favours SN1, because the carbocation is stable.
(Memory Note) SN1 goes through a carbocation, so rearrangement is always possible.
(Memory Note) Watch stereochemistry, not just connectivity.
(Memory Note) Bromination is highly selective for the tertiary position.

(Memory Note) Charge per unit time, nothing more.
(Memory Note) Ampere is one of the seven SI base units.
(Memory Note) Instantaneous means at one exact moment.
(Memory Note) Area under a current-time graph is always charge.
(Memory Note) One over the time period is the frequency.
(Memory Note) Moving charge is the whole difference.
(Memory Note) Charge cannot pile up at a junction.

Charge From A Graph

  • The AREA UNDER the I-t curve gives the CHARGE

Current And Frequency

  • CURRENT AND FREQUENCY
  • I = charge by time period
  • One over the time period is the frequency
  • So I = charge into frequency
(Memory Note) Replace one over T with f and the formula simplifies.

ELECTROSTATICS vs CURRENT

  • ELECTROSTATICS vs CURRENT
  • If the charge is AT REST, that is called ELECTROSTATIC
  • If the charge is IN MOTION, that gives current
(Memory Note) Moving charge is the whole difference between the two chapters.
🃏

ELECTROSTATICS vs CURRENT

Kirchhoff Junction Rule

  • KIRCHHOFF JUNCTION RULE
  • The summation of the TOTAL INWARD CURRENT is equal to the summation of the TOTAL OUTWARD CURRENT
(Memory Note) Charge cannot pile up at a junction.
🃏
Image coming
CURRENT ELECTRICITY
Kirchhoff Junction Rule

What Is Electric Current

  • WHAT IS ELECTRIC CURRENT
  • Current is nothing but the RATE OF FLOW OF CHARGE
  • The unit is AMPERES
  • It is denoted by I
  • Instantaneous current I = dq by dt
(Memory Note) Charge per unit time — that is all current is.

One-pager

  • MAGNETIC EFFECTS OF CURRENT
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • MAGNETIC FLUX
  • Magnetic flux is B dot A
  • It is a dot product, so the flux is a scalar quantity
  • 2
  • UNIT OF MAGNETIC FIELD
  • The units of magnetic field are Tesla, denoted by T
  • 3
  • FORCE ON A CURRENT-CARRYING WIRE
  • F = B i l sine theta
  • Remember this formula throughout the chapter
  • 4
  • STRENGTH FROM FIELD LINES
  • If the magnetic field lines are crowded or denser, the field is strong
  • If the lines are less crowded or less dense, the field is weak
(Memory Note) Only the component of B perpendicular to the area contributes.
(Memory Note) Tesla is the SI unit of magnetic field.
(Memory Note) The sine theta means orientation matters.
(Memory Note) Crowded lines mean a strong field.

Magnetic Flux

  • MAGNETIC FLUX
  • Magnetic flux = B DOT A
  • It is a DOT PRODUCT, so the flux is a SCALAR quantity
(Memory Note) Only the component of B perpendicular to the area contributes to flux.

Reading Field Line Density

  • READING FIELD LINE DENSITY
  • If the magnetic field lines are CROWDED or DENSER, we call them STRONG magnetic field lines
  • If the lines are LESS CROWDED or less dense, the field is WEAK
(Memory Note) Crowded lines mean a strong field.

  • CHEMICAL KINETICS
  • JEE Crash · GenZ 2.O
  • 1
  • RATE OF REACTION
  • How many reactants are converted into products per unit time
  • 2
  • RATE FROM CONCENTRATION
  • Final concentration minus initial concentration, by time taken
  • Rate is concentration change per unit time
  • 3
  • RATE IN CALCULUS FORM
  • Rate = minus dA by dt, where A is the reactant
  • 4
  • AVERAGE RATE
  • Final concentration minus initial concentration, divided by total time taken
  • 5
  • RATE EQUATION
  • The equation linking rate to concentration
  • 6
  • ZERO ORDER REACTION
  • Rate = k
  • Anything to the power 0 is 1
  • 7
  • ZERO ORDER GRAPH
  • A naught is the intercept
  • Slope = minus k
(Memory Note) The minus sign in minus dA by dt is because the reactant is being used up.

  • Angular momentum is equal to an INTEGRAL MULTIPLE of h by 2 pi
  • n must be an INTEGER

Rutherford Scattering Formula

  • RUTHERFORD SCATTERING FORMULA
  • N = k z SQUARE upon SINE TO THE POWER 4 of theta by 2
  • k is a constant
  • z is the atomic number
  • theta is the angle at which it is scattering
(Memory Note) The sine is raised to the fourth power — that is the easiest part to get wrong.

What Rutherford Saw

  • WHAT RUTHERFORD SAW
  • MOST of the alpha particles go UNDEVIATED
  • SOME deviate at an angle
  • Some scatter completely at 180 DEGREES
(Memory Note) Mostly empty space, with a tiny dense core at the centre.

Why Scattering Happens

  • WHY SCATTERING HAPPENS
  • An ALPHA PARTICLE is a positive particle
  • There is a POSITIVE CHARGE inside the nucleus
(Memory Note) Like charges repel, and that repulsion is what turns the alpha particle.

Fractional Atomic Mass

  • A1N1 plus A2N2 plus A3N3, divided by the total
  • A is the mass of each isotope
  • N is the PERCENTAGE of that isotope

One-pager

  • MAGNETISM AND MATTER
  • JEE Crash · Quick Revision
  • 1
  • MAGNETIC MOMENT OF A LOOP
  • The magnetic moment is equal to I dot A
  • 2
  • MAGNETIC MOMENT OF A BAR MAGNET
  • Write pole strength in place of charge
  • Multiply by the distance between the poles, which is 2L
  • 3
  • FIELD LINES NEVER INTERSECT
  • Two magnetic field lines will never intersect each other
  • 4
  • DIPOLE ORIENTATION
  • If the field and the dipole moment are in opposite directions, take the angle as 180 degrees
  • 5
  • AT A RANDOM POINT
  • A point that is neither on the axis nor on the equatorial line needs the general case
(Memory Note) Current times area, as a dot product.
(Memory Note) Pole strength takes the place of charge for a magnet.
(Memory Note) Crossing lines would mean two field directions at one point.
(Memory Note) The angle between them decides the sign.
(Memory Note) Axis and equator are the two easy cases.

Dipole Orientation

  • DIPOLE ORIENTATION
  • If the field and the dipole moment are in OPPOSITE directions, take the angle as 180 DEGREES
(Memory Note) The angle between field and moment decides the sign of the result.

Field Lines Never Intersect

  • FIELD LINES NEVER INTERSECT
  • Two magnetic field lines will NEVER intersect each other
(Memory Note) Crossing would mean two field directions at one point, which is impossible.

  • MAGNETIC MOMENT OF A BAR MAGNET
  • Write POLE STRENGTH in the place of charge
  • Multiply by the DISTANCE BETWEEN THEM, which is 2L
